routes.description: Establish a cumulative historical inference from bodily appearance testimony, the empty tomb, witness transformations, and comparative miracle evidence to Jesus's physical resurrection.
routes.successCriteria: The combined evidence must make a physical resurrection a historically reasonable explanation with greater explanatory unity than the proposed visionary, literary, relocation, or theft alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative historical evidence specifically to Jesus returning bodily from death.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the earliest appearance traditions concern an embodied Jesus and include individual and group encounters.
Establish a known burial followed by a genuinely missing body that natural alternatives do not explain as economically.
Connect sincere testimony, costly proclamation, and prominent conversions to experiences requiring a historical explanation.
Show that rival miracle traditions and visionary models do not match the relevant resurrection evidence closely enough to neutralize it.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply historically credible transmission through Paul, Luke, and restrained canonical narratives.
Keep supernatural causation available as a historical explanatory category rather than excluding it in advance.

routes.description: Show that the surviving testimony is too indirect, ambiguous, and comparable to rival religious claims to warrant a historical conclusion of physical resurrection.
routes.successCriteria: The evidence must remain compatible with visionary development, literary construction, ordinary movement dynamics, or natural tomb histories without requiring Jesus's bodily return from death.

motionBridge.description: Prevent the available historical record from warranting the specific conclusion that Jesus physically rose from death.

centralBridges.description: Establish the absence of secure firsthand corroboration for group encounters with a physically resurrected Jesus.
Show that early visionary ambiguity and later narrative elaboration can account for the appearance traditions.
Demonstrate that comparable miracle witnesses, persecution, and movement growth do not reliably discriminate supernatural truth.
Keep relocation, theft, uncertain burial, or literary construction available as explanations of the tomb traditions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require evidence that informed witnesses suffered specifically for firsthand belief in a bodily resurrection.
Identify independent corroboration as a missing support for the reported postmortem appearances.

sections.title: Appearance testimony and bodily resurrection
sections.rationale: The motion requires not merely survival or religious experience but a physical resurrection, making the content and historical basis of the reported appearances indispensable.

sections.title: Source access and visionary interpretation
sections.rationale: The inference depends on whether the surviving sources provide reliable access to public encounters or remain compatible with visionary experiences and later transmission.

sections.title: Rival miracle claims and comparative standards
sections.rationale: Comparisons with Mormon and other miracle traditions test whether the evidential standards applied to Christian testimony discriminate the resurrection claim without special pleading.

sections.title: Sincerity, conversion, and persecution
sections.rationale: Conversions and costly proclamation matter only insofar as they connect informed sincerity and witness access to the specific claim of bodily resurrection.

sections.title: Empty tomb and natural alternatives
sections.rationale: A missing body supplies a distinct route toward bodily resurrection, while burial uncertainty, relocation, theft, and narrative construction provide competing explanations.
